claims.text: CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational screening can be used to design high-entropy alloys.
Using CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening will improve phase stability relative to conventional alloy design.
Using CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening will refine HEA microstructures relative to conventional alloy design.
Using CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening will enhance material properties relative to conventional alloy design.
The initial HEA system contains a mixture of phases and possible elemental segregation.
CALPHAD can be integrated with high-throughput calculations and multi-objective optimization algorithms for HEA design.
A compositional search range of 5–50 at.% for each element can be used in high-throughput CALPHAD screening.
Parallel computational resources are required to manage the large data sets generated by the screening.
CALPHAD calculations generate phase predictions and thermophysical descriptors such as mixing enthalpy, atomic-size difference, and the omega parameter.
Mixing enthalpy, atomic-size difference, and the omega parameter are associated with the ability of an HEA to form a single phase.
CALPHAD uses thermodynamic databases and models to simulate phase equilibria through free-energy minimization.
The calculations can identify conditions under which a predominant single-phase solid solution forms.
Identifying single-phase formation conditions guides microstructure refinement and optimizes mechanical or functional properties.
CALPHAD-designed HEAs will have a dominant single-phase microstructure with fewer undesired intermetallic phases.
The reduction of undesired intermetallic phases will improve mechanical and functional properties.
Traditional empirical alloy design requires extensive trial-and-error and tends to produce less-controlled multiphase microstructures and suboptimal properties.
The effectiveness of CALPHAD screening depends on the availability and quality of thermodynamic databases.
CALPHAD screening may become computationally challenging for systems containing more than five principal elements.
The magnitude of improvement is uncertain and depends on database accuracy and processing details.
A controlled comparison using XRD, SEM/TEM, tensile strength, and hardness can test whether CALPHAD-designed alloys outperform empirically designed alloys.
